Storage efficiency

The messages being passed around and persisted are binary formatted and tiny. There are several points where data is passed around or persisted:

  • Process execution administration: keeps a working record of a process instance required to further process it. This is persisted in Kafka Topics and changelogs in the Kafka cluster for all process instances until they have been completed after which the data is purged. The engine nodes keep these cached in memory. After a restart the memory is restored from the changelogs
  • Output stream: this is a stream of data representing what happened to process instances and flow nodes and can be read by consumers with specific purposes. This data is retained for a configurable period of time.

For example for the process definitions used in this test this was the amount of data persisted in the Kafka cluster:

  • For the minimal trivial process definition:
    • Process execution administration: 100 bytes per process instance
    • Output stream: 400 bytes per finished process instance
  • For the “typical” process definition (started with approximately 100 byte variable payload)
    • Process execution administration: 9kB
    • Output stream: 3kB

If we take the “typical” process definition; what this eﬀectively means is that an engine node with 8GB of memory is theoretically able to administer and process over 900,000 active process instances in memory at any one time. If we need more we can add nodes but we can also choose to persist to disk allowing for much more at the cost of a bit performance.

For running instances a single Kafka node with a 150GB disk could store process instance information for over 13 million active process instances (including the output stream). So with a cluster of three that would increase to around 40 million. Kafka will remove old/stale data after a configurable retention period. When configured correctly this will eﬀectively increase that number even more.
